title: What do you believe about learning?

files.lesson.md:
---
order: 1
unit: believe
title: What do you believe about learning?
summary: "Everyone has beliefs about learning, like 'smart people find it easy' or 'if it looks familiar, I know it'. Beliefs like these steer what you do: whether you keep going, check your work or give up. Some of them are often wrong. Noticing your beliefs, and changing what you do because of them, is part of being your own learning coach."
language: science
shape: primer
hook: "If you're smart, learning should feel easy. Agree or disagree?"
---
There are no right answers in the first step. Everyone else in this workshop is made up.

## Think first

```step
stage: predict
insight: "Getting students' own beliefs about learning out in the open before anything is named. No answer is marked; the reasons are what matter."
check:
  type: reflect
  text: "I've decided whether I agree, disagree or I'm not sure for each statement, and I have a reason for at least one."
```

For each statement, decide: **agree**, **disagree** or **not sure**. Have a reason ready for at least one of them.

1. If you're smart, learning should feel easy.
2. If you have to work hard at something, you're probably not good at it.
3. If something looks familiar, you know it.
4. Some people are just maths people, and some aren't.
5. If you get it quickly, you've learned it.
6. Mistakes mean you're doing it wrong.

You'll come back to these at the end, privately.

## The idea

```step
stage: investigate
insight: "Beliefs aren't just opinions: they steer what a learner does next. Then a planted slip: slow means not good at it."
tasks:
  - insight: "Linking a belief to what it makes someone do."
    check:
      type: match
      q: "Each made-up learner has a belief about learning. Match it to what it might make them do."
      pairs:
        - ["Zara believes smart people find it easy.", "When a question gets hard, she decides she's not smart and stops."]
        - ["Omar believes that if it looks familiar, he knows it.", "He rereads his notes instead of testing himself."]
        - ["Lucy believes she's 'not a maths person'.", "She guesses instead of checking, because what's the point?"]
        - ["Theo believes mistakes mean you're doing it wrong.", "He hides his working so nobody sees his mistakes."]
  - check:
      type: bug
      code: "working.txt#nib"
      text: "Nib is doing a maths question. Click the line where Nib's thinking first goes wrong."
      answer: 3
      fault: logic
      misconception: fast-means-smart
      explain: "Line 3: taking longer than a friend doesn't mean Nib is bad at maths. It means this question takes Nib more steps right now. Working through it is how Nib gets faster."
```

Everyone has beliefs about learning, and they **steer what you do**: whether you keep going, check your work, try another way or give up. Zara stops. Omar rereads. Lucy guesses. Theo hides his working.

Some common beliefs are often wrong:

- **Fast means smart.** How quickly you get something says little about how well you'll learn it. Lots of things feel slow at first.
- **Hard work means you're not good at it.** Effort is often how learning happens. Things that felt hard last year probably feel easier now.
- **Familiar means known.** Recognising something on the page is easier than doing it without the page. (Workshop 4 is all about this one.)
- **Mistakes mean you're doing it wrong.** Mistakes usually show you where to work next.

None of this means anyone can learn anything instantly, or that effort alone is enough. You usually get better at things with practice **and** good strategies, and some things take a long time.

This course is about **self-regulated learning**, which here means **being your own learning coach**: noticing what's going on in your learning (your thinking, how you feel, why you're doing it, what you're doing) and changing what you do when it isn't working. Noticing a belief that's steering you the wrong way is one of the coach's jobs. The next workshop is all about the coach.

## Check

```step
stage: practise
tasks:
  - insight: "Sorting statements about learning by what research usually finds. These ones have clearer answers than the opening statements."
    check:
      type: sort
      q: "Sort each statement: is it usually true, or often misleading?"
      options: ["Usually true", "Often misleading"]
      items:
        - ["You can get better at most things with practice and good strategies.", "Usually true"]
        - ["How fast you get something shows how smart you are.", "Often misleading"]
        - ["If it feels hard, you're learning nothing.", "Often misleading", "Hard work is often where the learning happens."]
        - ["Checking without your notes shows what you really know.", "Usually true"]
        - ["A mistake often shows you where to work next.", "Usually true"]
        - ["Some people just can't learn maths.", "Often misleading", "People differ, but most people can get better at maths with practice and help."]
  - check:
      type: question
      q: "Ella has been on a science question for ten minutes. She thinks, \"This is taking ages, so I must be bad at science.\" What would her learning coach say?"
      options: ["\"Taking a while doesn't mean I'm bad at it. Which part is slowing me down?\"", "\"Yep, science isn't for me. I'll skip to the next one.\"", "\"Everyone else is faster, so I should just copy them.\"", "\"If I was any good at this, it would be easy by now.\""]
      answer: 0
      feedback: [null, "That's the belief talking, not the coach.", "Comparing and copying skips the learning.", "That's the 'smart means easy' belief again."]
      explain: "The coach notices the belief and turns it into a question about what to do next."
```

### Ella's coach

## Apply

```step
stage: make
insight: "Students turn the idea on themselves, privately. Share only what you're comfortable with."
check:
  type: reflect
  text: "I've looked back at the six statements and thought about whether my answers have changed."
```

Look back at the six statements from the start. Just for yourself:

- Did you agree with any of the ones that are often misleading? Has your answer changed?
- Think of a subject where learning feels slow or hard for you. Next time it does, what could your coach say instead of "I'm bad at this"?

You don't need to share any of this. If you want to, share one reason with your partner.

```teacher
summary: Students take a position on six beliefs about learning (no right
  answers), match made-up learners' beliefs to what those beliefs make them do,
  find Nib's slip (slower than a friend, so bad at maths), sort statements by
  what research usually finds, and write the learning coach's reply to an
  unhelpful belief. The workshop names self-regulated learning as being your own
  learning coach. Students finish by privately looking back at their own
  answers.
time: 40
timing: Think first 8 min · The idea 14 min · Check 8 min · Apply 5 min (plus
  the class discussion)
goals:
  - I can explain how a belief about learning can change what I do.
  - I can name a common belief about learning that is often wrong, and say why.
  - I can say what being my own learning coach means.
struggle: "Some students will strongly agree with 'some people are just maths
  people', often from their own experience. Don't argue them out of it: ask what
  that belief makes someone do, and whether that helps."
before: >
  **Why beliefs first.** Students already have beliefs about learning, so the
  course starts by drawing them out before naming anything (elicit, then teach).
  Beliefs about learning are one of the lenses Barr uses to look at
  self-regulated learning; the specific beliefs here come from research on
  epistemic beliefs (Schommer: quick learning, fixed ability) and on illusions
  of competence and desirable difficulties (Bjork).


  **Kept honest on mindset.** The lesson doesn't promise that believing you can
  grow is enough. Large reviews find growth mindset interventions have small
  average effects, larger for some groups (Sisk and colleagues 2018; Yeager and
  colleagues 2019). The claim here is narrower and better supported: beliefs
  steer behaviour (giving up, rereading, guessing), and practice with good
  strategies usually helps. Keep "usually" and "often".


  **The definition.** Self-regulated learning means understanding and adjusting
  your own thinking, motivation, emotions and behaviour in learning (Barr).
  Students meet it as "being your own learning coach", and workshop 2 builds the
  coach in full.


  **No right answers in Think first.** Accept every reasoned view. The Check
  sort uses clearer statements than the opening six on purpose.


  **Personal reflection.** Apply asks students to look back at their own answers
  privately. They share only what they're comfortable with, and the class
  discussion stays on the made-up learners. Nothing is collected.
running:
  - "Think first: run it as a line across the room (agree at one end, disagree
    at the other) for two or three statements. Ask for reasons from both ends."
  - "The idea: after the match, ask what Zara, Omar, Lucy and Theo could each
    believe instead, and what they'd do then."
  - "The idea: read the definition aloud and write 'be your own learning coach'
    on the board for the rest of the course."
  - Apply is private. Don't ask which statements students agreed with.
stuck:
  - see: A student says some people really are better at maths.
    ask: Maybe. Does believing 'I'm not a maths person' help someone get better, or
      stop them trying?
    fix: People differ. The belief to watch is the one that stops you trying.
  - see: A student thinks the lesson is saying effort is all you need.
    ask: If someone tries hard with a strategy that doesn't work, what happens?
    fix: Effort plus good strategies, and sometimes help. Workshop 5 is about
      strategies.
  - see: A student is upset about a subject they find hard.
    ask: What's one small part of it you've got better at?
    fix: Hard now doesn't mean hard forever. Follow up privately if it seems to
      matter more than the lesson.
stretch: Pick one of the six statements and write a better version, one you
  think is usually true.
support: "Three beliefs on a card with what to say instead: fast means smart →
  slow can mean learning; hard means bad at it → hard can mean learning;
  mistakes are bad → mistakes show where to work."
leads: >
  Next: your learning coach. Whoever chose the task, you plan, check and look
  back.


  Links: When easy fools you (workshop 4) takes the 'familiar means known'
  belief further.
exit:
  q: Name one belief about learning that's often wrong, and what it might make
    someone do.
  a: Any reasoned pair, such as 'fast means smart', which might make someone give
    up when a task is slow.
explain: >
  Everyone has **beliefs about learning**, and they steer what you do: keep
  going, check, try another way, or give up.


  Some common ones are often wrong: **fast means smart**, **hard work means
  you're not good at it**, **familiar means known**, and **mistakes mean you're
  doing it wrong**.


  Being your own **learning coach** means noticing what's going on in your
  learning, beliefs included, and changing what you do when it isn't working.
class:
  inquiry:
    q: Where do our beliefs about learning come from?
    prompts:
      - Things people say to you, like 'you're a natural'?
      - How fast other people seem to get things?
      - Marks?
    notes: Keep it general. The aim is to notice that beliefs are learned, so they
      can change. Nobody has to say what they believe.
  activities:
    - at: predict
      kind: activity
      title: Take a stand
      minutes: 8
      do: >
        Agree at one end of the room, disagree at the other, not sure in the
        middle. Move for each statement your teacher reads out. Be ready to give
        a reason.
      notes: Do two or three of the six. Ask for reasons from both ends and let people
        move if they're persuaded. Students can stay in the middle if they'd
        rather not say. This is the only time the class shares a position on
        their own beliefs, and it's on general statements.
    - at: end
      kind: discussion
      title: Zara's coach
      minutes: 5
      do: >
        In pairs: Zara stops when a question gets hard. Write one thing her
        learning coach could say to her.
      notes: "Take a few aloud. Good ones turn the belief into a next step: 'Hard
        means I'm learning. Which part is hard?'"
  questions:
    - at: investigate
      title: What would they do?
      type: question
      q: Ari believes mistakes mean you're doing it wrong. What might Ari do in a
        test?
      options:
        - Leave questions blank rather than risk a wrong answer
        - Check every answer twice
        - Ask for help more often
      answer: 0
      explain: If mistakes feel like proof you're bad at it, avoiding them can matter
        more than learning.
```
